title: Beyond Bond Gauge: Exact Tensor-Network Tangent Spaces at Weighted Graph States
abstract: For normal PEPS, the fundamental theorem settles at the finite level whether virtual-bond gauge exhausts a tensor network's representation freedom. We ask the first-order question at a fixed representation, from both sides of the differential: which tensor variations leave the state unchanged without being bond gauges, and which physical directions can no variation reach? We answer both exactly for weighted graph state (WGS) tensor networks with equal physical and bond dimension $q\ge2$, which include the graph-state resources of measurement-based quantum computation. Dividing a single-tensor variation by the nonvanishing amplitude turns it into an arbitrary function on the closed neighborhood of its vertex. Overlapping neighborhoods give the complete kernel. Its non-bond part is generated on periodic regular-polygon tilings by triangles, chordless squares, and edge-sharing diamonds. Under stated period conditions, generic gauge completeness on all thirty-nine families studied identifies this nullity as a WGS rank drop: for thirty-three families at every $q\ge2$, and for six at $q=2$. Supports outside every neighborhood give the missing directions: at qubit graph states on the eleven Archimedean tilings every nearest-neighbor $XX$ and $YY$ direction is missing, including on honeycomb, where the non-bond kernel is empty. On large honeycomb and square tori, small nonzero coherent $XX$ errors leave the bond-two PEPS set on the same graph. Removing redundant parameters and supplying missing directions are therefore distinct operations.
summary: This work provides an exact, first-order analysis of the representation freedom within Weighted Graph State tensor networks. It precisely identifies the mathematical structures responsible for parameter redundancy (the non-bond kernel) and the physical limitations (missing directions) of the state space. This is crucial for understanding the underlying mathematical constraints governing quantum states in condensed matter physics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the first-order representation freedom of tensor networks, specifically determining which tensor variations leave the state unchanged without being simple bond gauges, and identifying unreachable physical directions.
main_result: For Weighted Graph States, the non-bond kernel is generated by motifs like triangles and chordless squares, and the analysis quantifies the rank drop associated with gauge completeness across various periodic tilings.
method: The authors use differential calculus on the parameter space of tensor networks, analyzing the kernel and image of the contraction differential map to characterize redundant parameters and the physical tangent space.
model_or_system: The model is the Weighted Graph State (WGS) represented by PEPS (Projected Entangled Pair States) tensor networks, which are used to describe quantum states relevant to measurement-based quantum computation.
key_observables: Non-bond kernel generators, physical tangent space dimension, gauge completeness rank drop, and missing nearest-neighbor XX/YY directions.
important_parameters: Physical and bond dimension $q \ge 2$, and the structure of the underlying graph (e.g., honeycomb, square tori).
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed at a fixed, generic representation (first-order differential level) and relies on specific periodic boundary conditions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of the kernel (redundant parameters) and missing directions (uncovered support) using graph motifs and vertex neighborhoods.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the differential map for WGS, calculating the kernel (redundancy) and the image (physical space), and then characterizing the non-bond nullity and the missing directions separately.
why_interesting: The rigorous characterization of the tangent space and gauge redundancies in tensor network representations provides deep insights into the mathematical structure of quantum states, which is fundamental for simulating strongly correlated electron systems.
